candidate.answerReason: Bernardo certainly wins when he chooses 9. Otherwise the two players have identical independent selection distributions, with tie probability 1/56, giving an overall winning probability of 37/56.

methods.label: Separate the extra digit and use symmetry
methods.explanation:
Arranging a chosen triple in descending order determines exactly one number, so we should count unordered triples. Bernardo has \(\binom{9}{3}=84\) equally likely triples, and Silvia has \(\binom{8}{3}=56\).

If Bernardo chooses \(9\), his hundreds digit exceeds Silvia's, so he certainly wins. There are \(\binom{8}{2}=28\) such triples, giving probability \(28/84=1/3\).

With the remaining probability \(2/3\), Bernardo does not choose \(9\). In this case both players independently choose uniformly from the same \(56\) triples. For each Bernardo triple, exactly one Silvia triple produces a tie, so the conditional tie probability is \(1/56\). Swapping the players' triples reversibly pairs every Bernardo win with a Silvia win. Therefore the remaining probability is split equally between them:
\[
\Pr(\text{Bernardo wins}\mid\text{no }9)
=\frac{1-1/56}{2}=\frac{55}{112}.
\]
The cases of choosing and not choosing \(9\) are disjoint and exhaustive. Hence the requested probability is
\[
\frac13+\frac23\cdot\frac{55}{112}
=\boxed{\frac{37}{56}},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
methods.levelReason: The argument uses combinations, elementary conditional probabilities, and a reversible pairing of equally likely outcomes.

candidate.annotationRationale: The task concerns probability in finite equally likely selection spaces. Combinations supply the selection counts. Conditioning on the extra digit and pairing reversed outcomes are the actual method components; ties must be removed before applying symmetry.
